facts.text: This film was originally titled Tucker and Flynn, after its two cop leads. Moria's review guesses it was renamed to dodge comparison to Turner & Hooch (1989).
Critic Adrian Martin says Monolith kicks off a cycle of movies inspired by The X-Files, and gave it two stars out of five.
Director John Eyres and Geoff Griffiths of EGM Film International built the script around a pre-sale concept. Writer Stephen Lister turned it into the screenplay.
No monoliths appear in Monolith. Moria's Richard Scheib jokes the title is inaccurate, and critic Christian Sauvé called it 'misleading' in his 1997 review.
The Schlock Pit's Matty Budrewicz says this was director John Eyres' American debut and EGM's most expensive-looking production up to that point.
Moria's Richard Scheib found the name of John Hurt's character, Villano, laughably unsubtle. It's a hair away from 'villain.'
Director John Eyres made Project: Shadowchaser (1992) just before this. Moria's reviewer called Monolith 'marginally more credible' than that earlier sci-fi film.
Monolith's prosthetic makeup artist Howard Berger later won the Best Makeup Oscar for The Chronicles of Narnia: The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe (2005).
Eyres later directed two Project: Shadowchaser sequels, then Judge and Jury (1996), the giant-sea-monster flick Octopus (2000) and Ripper: Letter from Hell (2001).
The Introvision front-projection system used on Monolith debuted on Outland (1981). It also helped make Darkman (1990), Army of Darkness (1992) and The Fugitive (1993).
Makeup effects came from Howard Berger, who later co-founded KNB EFX Group. Visual effects used Introvision, a front-projection process, supervised by John Mesa.
Introvision was invented by John Eppolito, a stage magician and hypnotist. The process faded around 1994 as digital compositing took over, so Monolith came near the end of its run.
John Hurt played the lead in Alien (1979) and here plays Villano. Moria's review called him miscast as a villain: his small stature and delivery undercut the menace.
Musetta Vander (Dr. Katya Pavlova) went on to play Sindel in Mortal Kombat Annihilation (1997) and a Siren in the Coen brothers' O Brother, Where Art Thou? (2000).
Moria's review called the secret-government-agency plot a clichéd bid to cash in on The X-Files. It says the agency gets more screen time than the alien.
Musetta Vander (Dr. Katya Pavlova) also played the She-Mantis in Buffy the Vampire Slayer's 'Teacher's Pet' and guest-starred on Star Trek: Voyager.
Cinematographer Alan M. Trow was a regular collaborator of director John Eyres. The Schlock Pit praised the film's polished photography.
The Schlock Pit's Matty Budrewicz calls the film's score, by composer Frank Becker, bizarrely heavy on xylophone.
Star Bill Paxton had worked with John Hurt's Alien co-star Sigourney Weaver in Aliens (1986). Hurt and Paxton both appear here, one Alien franchise veteran apiece.
Louis Gossett Jr. (Capt. MacCandless) is also famous as Colonel Chappy Sinclair in the Iron Eagle movies, which ran from 1986 to 1995.
The Schlock Pit's Matty Budrewicz compares the premise, an alien that hops from body to body, to The Hidden (1987) and The Borrower (1991).
Louis Gossett Jr. was cast in Brian's Song (1971) but tore his Achilles days before shooting. Producer David Wolper promised him the next great role: Fiddler in Roots (1977), which won him an Emmy.
Louis Gossett Jr. won the Best Supporting Actor Oscar for An Officer and a Gentleman (1982). He was the first Black American to win in that category.
Lindsay Frost (Terri Flynn) also appeared in the vampire-cop movie Dead Heat (1988) and later in The Ring (2002).
Lindsay Frost's brothers are Mark Frost, co-creator of Twin Peaks, and writer Scott Frost. Her father was actor Warren Frost.
Paul Ganus (Connor) was also in Lethal Weapon 3 (1992) and later The Mask of Zorro (1998). He's a native of Midland, Michigan.
Lindsay Frost's son Lucas Giolito became a first-round MLB draft pick in 2012. He later pitched for the Cleveland Guardians.
Moria's Richard Scheib calls The Hidden (1987) the template for alien-possession cop movies, later followed by Peacemaker (1990) and I Come in Peace (1990).
Bill Paxton directed his own horror film, Frailty (2001), and starred in it. It earned him Saturn Award nominations for Best Director and Best Horror Film.
Film-O-Spheric likens the bickering between Bill Paxton's Tucker and Lindsay Frost's Terri Flynn to Dirty Harry, Hunter and Dempsey and Makepeace. The site calls it more buddy-cop movie than sci-fi.
Bill Paxton later starred in Nightcrawler (2014). The Nightcrawler of the X-Men comics is a different character entirely.
Critic Adrian Martin groups Monolith with modest straight-to-video films modeled on TV hits like Miami Vice, Moonlighting and Twin Peaks, not on big-screen hits.
In the UK, First Independent released the film in 1994 after the BBFC required 19 seconds of cuts.
Musetta Vander, who plays Dr. Katya Pavlova, was born Musetta van der Merwe in Durban, South Africa. Her first notable role was in the TV series Super Force (1991-92).
The film reached US video on February 23, 1994, through MCA Universal, according to The Schlock Pit.
John Hurt holds a Hollywood record for onscreen character deaths, 47 in all. He later played the War Doctor in Doctor Who.
Reviewing Monolith after an April 1997 TV airing, critic Christian Sauvé called it a 'bad and stupid SF thriller' with a 'brain-damagingly stupid' ending. His verdict: 'Avoid.'
The Schlock Pit's Matty Budrewicz called the film 'good, bad, boring, and brilliant' all at once, a tonal identity crisis.
Adrian Martin calls the film's opening 'wonderfully catastrophic.' He says the finale swaps the X-Files formula for a colorful homage to the Alien movies.
